final_proof:
Proof. Since M is locally Euclidean of dimension d, there is an open neighborhood W of m and a homeomorphism φ: W → V, where V is an open subset of ℝ^d. (If the definition initially supplies a not-necessarily-open neighborhood W₀, replace it by its interior W: because W₀ is a neighborhood of m, m lies in W; moreover, W is open in the subspace W₀, so its image under the given homeomorphism is open in ℝ^d, and the restricted map is the required chart.) Put x = φ(m). Because V is open and x ∈ V, there is a real number ρ > 0 such that the open Euclidean ball B(x,ρ) is contained in V.

For every positive integer n, define

U_n = φ⁻¹(B(x,ρ/n)).

The ball B(x,ρ/n) is open in V, and φ is a homeomorphism, so U_n is open in W. Since W is open in M, U_n is open in M as well. Also m ∈ U_n. Thus every U_n is an open neighborhood of m. Furthermore, the restriction φ|_{U_n}: U_n → B(x,ρ/n) is a homeomorphism. Equivalently, its inverse maps the open ball B(x,ρ/n) homeomorphically onto U_n, so each U_n is a homeomorphic image of an open ball in ℝ^d.

It remains to prove the local-basis property. Let A be any neighborhood of m in M. By the definition of neighborhood, there is an open set G in M such that m ∈ G ⊆ A (if neighborhoods are defined to be open, simply take G = A). The set G ∩ W is open in W and contains m. Hence φ(G ∩ W) is an open subset of V containing x. Since V itself is open in ℝ^d, φ(G ∩ W) is open in ℝ^d. Therefore, for some δ > 0,

B(x,δ) ⊆ φ(G ∩ W).

Choose a positive integer n large enough that ρ/n < δ. Then

U_n = φ⁻¹(B(x,ρ/n)) ⊆ φ⁻¹(B(x,δ)) ⊆ G ∩ W ⊆ A.

Thus every neighborhood A of m contains some U_n. Consequently (U_n)_{n≥1} is a local basis at m. It is indexed by the positive integers and hence is countable, and every one of its members is homeomorphic to an open ball of ℝ^d, as required. This argument also covers d = 0, where ℝ^0 and each of its nonempty open balls consist of one point.
